cats.name: Social actors
cats.def: How people and institutions are included or excluded, activated or passivated, named or classified, and made specific or generic.
cats.ask: Who acts upon whom, and who is absent from the clause?

cats.name: Nominalisation
cats.def: Processes represented as nouns, which can remove the agent and the time of the process from the clause.
cats.ask: Which processes become things, and whose agency disappears with them?

cats.name: Deontic modality
cats.def: Commitment to obligation or permission, expressed through modal verbs and through adjectives and nouns such as ‘required’ or ‘pre-requisite’.
cats.ask: Who is obliged or permitted, and by whom?

cats.name: Epistemic modality
cats.def: Commitment to truth, ranging from categorical assertion to hedged or attributed claims.
cats.ask: How strongly does the text commit to what it claims?

cats.name: Evaluation
cats.def: Evaluative statements and attributes, together with affective mental processes such as fear or concern.
cats.ask: What is presented as good or bad, and on whose authority?

cats.name: Semantic relations
cats.def: Relations between clauses and sentences, such as reason, consequence, purpose, condition, contrast and time.
cats.ask: How are refusal and loss connected in the grammar?

cats.name: Assumptions
cats.def: What the text takes as given. Fairclough separates assumptions about existence and about what is the case from assumptions about value.
cats.ask: What must the reader already accept for the sentence to make sense?

cats.name: Reporting and intertextuality
cats.def: How other voices enter the text, whether quoted, paraphrased, left unattributed or held at a distance by scare quotes.
cats.ask: Whose words are these, and how close does the text stand to them?

cats.name: Legitimation
cats.def: Justification by authority, by utility, by moral value or by narrative, following Van Leeuwen’s strategies as Fairclough presents them.
cats.ask: On what grounds is the condition justified?

cats.name: Wording
cats.def: Choices of vocabulary and naming that identify a discourse and classify people and places.
cats.ask: Which words name the people and the place?

docs.title: UNHCR, Guidance on Registration and Identity Management, section 5.2, ‘Registration as an Identity Management Process’
docs.voice: UNHCR operational guidance addressed to registration staff. Several sentences tell the interviewer what to say to the person being registered.
docs.profile: The section makes the individual the grammatical holder of a right to refuse and defines consent as a genuine choice without adverse consequences. The same list places an obligation to cooperate beside the reminder of voluntariness. In a footnote, the guidance then assigns the requirement to share data, together with the right to object, to government policy wherever a government leads registration.

ex.t: Individuals should be reminded that participation in registration is voluntary;
ex.v: Guidance to staff, in the list headed ‘Rights and obligations of individuals’.

a.n: People appear as a generic class and as the object of reminding, while the staff member who reminds them stays implicit in the passive.
The median deontic ‘should’ places the duty to remind on staff, which makes voluntariness something the interviewer must state.
The nominalisation turns the act of registering into a state that can carry the attribute ‘voluntary’, with no agency named as the one asking.
The unmodalised present asserts voluntariness as a fact about registration, the attribute that the Bangladesh notice replaces with ‘required’ in the same frame.

ex.t: Individuals should be advised about their obligation to cooperate and give truthful and complete responses to the questions asked;
ex.v: Guidance to staff, the next item in the same list.

a.n: Placed directly after the reminder of voluntariness, the obligation appears as a noun that the individual possesses, and the agency that demands cooperation is left unstated.
The demand for truthful and complete answers presupposes that answers could be otherwise, an assumption that the verification texts in the cases make explicit.

ex.t: Individuals have the right to refuse the collection of their biometrics on legitimate grounds related to his or her specific personal situation.
ex.v: Guidance to staff, same list.

a.n: The individual is the activated holder of a right to refuse, and the node is the only text in the core corpus where refusal belongs to the person as a right.
The nominalisation names the collecting without a collector, so the right is directed at a process whose agent is absent.
The same adjective qualifies the host government’s ‘interest in knowing who is on its territory’ a few paragraphs later.
The qualification assumes that refusal needs grounds and that someone other than the person judges their legitimacy, locating those grounds in individual circumstances.

ex.t: This does not alter their right to international protection and the individual remains of concern to UNHCR.
ex.v: Guidance to staff, the sentence that follows the right to refuse.

a.n: A categorical negative in the present tense guarantees that refusal leaves protection intact, with no condition attached.
The assurance presupposes that a reader might expect refusal to affect protection, which is the link that the operational texts go on to make.
The phrase keeps the refuser inside the agency’s mandate category, so refusal leaves the person’s institutional status unchanged.

ex.t: In such cases, individuals may be registered, and alternative methods identified to ensure they can access rights, assistance and solutions.
ex.v: Guidance to staff, the sentence after the assurance.

a.n: The low modal ‘may’ permits registration without biometrics and leaves the decision with the operation.
The elliptical passive leaves open who identifies the alternatives and who bears the work of finding them.
The purpose relation ties refusal to continued access, the relation that the Bangladesh notice and FAQ replace with consequence.

ex.t: Where the host government leads registration procedures, the requirement to share personal data including biometrics (and the related right to object) may be determined according to government policy, not UNHCR policy.
ex.v: Footnote 5 of the section.

a.n: The conditional clause names the case in which the guidance defers to a government, the arrangement found in Bangladesh and Malaysia.
The obligation to share is a noun with no stated source, so the requirement exists in the sentence before any agent imposes it.
The right to object appears in brackets as an appendage of the requirement, a typographic subordination of the person’s right.
The modal passive leaves open both whether and by whom the matter is decided.
The closing contrast removes the agency’s own policy from the case, so the footnote marks the point where the node’s standard stops applying.

ex.t: The host government has a legitimate interest in knowing who is on its territory
ex.v: Content the interviewer ‘should further explain’ to the person when seeking consent to share data.

a.n: The government is the activated holder of an interest, the grammatical role the individual holds as bearer of a right to refuse.
The attribute evaluates the government’s interest positively, using the adjective that elsewhere restricts the individual’s grounds for refusal.
Knowledge of presence is nominalised as the object of the interest, a phrase the 2026 FAQ from Bangladesh restates as ‘authorities know who has arrived on their territory’.

ex.t: Freely given means that the individual has a genuine choice and is able to refuse or withdraw without adverse consequences.
ex.v: Guidance on consent to share personal information.

a.n: The definitional frame fixes the meaning of consent inside the guidance and makes the definition available for citation by other texts.
The attribute ‘genuine’ presupposes that a choice can exist in name only, the possibility that UNICEF later calls an ‘impossible choice’.
The individual is the subject of every process in the definition, holding the choice and performing refusal or withdrawal.
The phrase detaches refusal from loss, the relation that the Bangladesh texts and the South African texts reverse.

docs.title: UNHCR Bangladesh, ‘Registration Update Exercise Notice’
docs.voice: UNHCR Bangladesh notice addressed to registered refugees in the camps, setting out the registration update exercise.
docs.profile: The notice keeps the node’s nominalisation ‘participation’ and gives it the attribute ‘required’, then states the loss of all future assistance as a certain consequence of absence. The agencies that enrol and inactivate disappear behind agentless passives, while people appear as eligible persons or as persons who fail to show up.

ex.t: Biometrics will be enrolled for all individuals 5 years and above, given that establishing and preserving identities is key to ensuring protection and solutions for refugees.
ex.v: Notice, the paragraph after the stated purpose of the exercise.

a.n: The subject of the passive is ‘biometrics’, so the body’s measurements occupy the place of the person being enrolled.
The agentless passive with ‘will’ presents enrolment as scheduled fact and leaves the enrolling agencies unnamed.
People are classified by age alone, so children from the age of five enter the clause as subjects of enrolment.
The connective presents its reason as already granted, so the reader receives the justification as common ground.
Two gerunds name identity work without an agent who establishes or preserves.
Enrolment is legitimated by its utility for protection, an instrumental claim stated categorically.

ex.t: Participation in the exercise is required for all eligible persons.
ex.v: Notice, under the heading ‘ATTENDANCE’.

a.n: The node’s nominalisation returns in the same grammatical position, which makes the comparison with ‘participation in registration is voluntary’ direct.
The deontic ‘required’, which Fairclough (2003, p. 170) gives as a marker of obligation, takes the place of ‘voluntary’ and names no requiring agency.
The obligation falls on a generic class defined by eligibility, which the notice itself determines.

ex.t: Persons who fail to show up will be inactivated in the MRC, and they will not benefit from any assistance in future.
ex.v: Notice, under ‘ATTENDANCE’.

a.n: The relative clause defines people by a failure, which makes absence their own act and the first link in the sequence.
The agentless passive states deactivation of the record as certain and leaves the deactivating agency unnamed.
The quantifier ‘any’ and the phrase ‘in future’ give the loss no limit in scope or time.
The coordinated clause attaches a permanent loss of assistance to absence, the consequence relation that the node’s definition of consent excludes.

docs.title: Government of Bangladesh and UNHCR, ‘Frequently Asked Questions on Improved Data Processing Modalities’
docs.voice: Question and answer page published by UNHCR in the names of the Government of Bangladesh and UNHCR.
docs.profile: The FAQ sets protection beside the state’s knowledge of arrivals as purposes of equal rank. Refusal returns as a nominalised subject that ‘may lead’, through further nominalisations, to deregistration and the end of protection, with the deciding agencies absent from the chain.

ex.t: Registration and identification help ensure that people who need protection can be recognized and supported, and that authorities know who has arrived on their territory.
ex.v: Opening answer of the FAQ.

a.n: Two nominalisations occupy the subject position and do the helping, so no agency appears as the one who registers or identifies.
People are the passivated objects of recognition and support, defined by their need.
The coordinating ‘and’ gives the authorities’ knowledge of arrivals the same rank as protection, restating the node’s ‘legitimate interest in knowing who is on its territory’.

ex.t: Refugees’ obligations under international refugee law include adherence to local laws and a duty to provide accurate information.
ex.v: FAQ, same answer.

a.n: Obligation is nominalised and attributed to refugees as its possessors, which makes compliance a property of refugee status.
The duties are legitimated by the authority of international law, which the answer invokes in general terms.
Supplying data becomes a legal duty, a wording close to the node’s ‘obligation to cooperate and give truthful and complete responses’.

ex.t: a pre-requisite for the GoB’s protection and assistance
ex.v: FAQ, inside the reason clause that describes registration as a joint process of UNHCR and the Government of Bangladesh.

a.n: The noun states a condition without a modal verb, so obligation appears as a property of registration itself.
Protection and assistance are nominalised and owned by the government, which becomes their sole source in this clause.

ex.t: refusing the processing of personal data may lead to deregistration and, as a result, the discontinuation of protection and assistance depending on the circumstances.
ex.v: FAQ, the main clause after the reason clause.

a.n: The refuser is absorbed into a gerund and the refused process is itself nominalised, so refusal appears as an event with no person in it.
Epistemic ‘may’ softens a causal chain whose links are all nominalised, which lowers commitment while keeping the chain.
The outcome is named without a deregistering agent.
The explicit marker links refusal to the end of protection, the reverse of ‘without adverse consequences’ in the node.
A second nominalised outcome completes the chain, again with no agent who discontinues.
The closing hedge leaves the deciding criteria unstated.

docs.title: The Diplomat (Shafiur Rahman), ‘UNHCR Defends Biometric Enrollment Push for Rohingya Refugees’
docs.voice: News report on refugee families who refused enrolment, with UNHCR’s written replies quoted and paraphrased.
docs.profile: The report places the families’ refusal and the loss of food aid in a temporal sequence and keeps the agency of the cut-off implicit. The quoted replies legitimate enrolment by global standards and by the agency’s mandate, and they report an assessment of risk that has no named assessor.

ex.t: have been cut off from food aid and other essential services after refusing to participate in a biometric data collection drive.
ex.v: Lead sentence. The subject is ‘Around 300 to 400 Rohingya refugee families’ in the Nayapara and Kutupalong registered camps.

a.n: The journalist’s agentless passive leaves the agency that cut off food aid unnamed in the lead sentence.
A temporal connective places refusal before loss and leaves the causal link for the reader to infer.
The noun ‘drive’ presents enrolment as a campaign.
The families are the implied agents of refusal, the only clause in the core excerpts where people are reported as having refused.

ex.t: The letter stated that no humanitarian assistance could be provided to those not biometrically registered.
ex.v: Journalist paraphrasing UNHCR’s letter of 17 March, signed by its Head of Operations in Cox’s Bazar.

a.n: The agency’s letter reaches the reader in indirect speech, so its wording is the journalist’s paraphrase.
The negated ‘could’ with an agentless passive presents exclusion as an impossibility, with no provider named.
People are classified by a negative property, their absence from the biometric register.

ex.t: The use of biometrics in Bangladesh aligns with global standards for identity management and is essential for UNHCR to fulfill its mandate.
ex.v: UNHCR spokesperson, written reply quoted directly.

a.n: The nominalisation ‘use’ removes both the users and the persons whose biometrics are used.
Conformity with unnamed global standards legitimates the practice by external authority.
The adjective ‘essential’ grounds necessity in the agency’s mandate, so the institution’s needs justify the condition.

ex.t: no specific protection risks were identified
ex.v: UNHCR statement, quoted. The journalist adds that the claim concerned ‘suspending distributions’.

a.n: The qualifier narrows the claim to ‘specific’ risks, which leaves general risk unaddressed.
The agentless passive reports an assessment with no named assessor and no stated method.

docs.title: Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, ‘Safe, Transparent Aid for Gaza’ (overview memo)
docs.voice: The foundation’s own overview memo, written in the first person plural and in lists of activities and inputs.
docs.profile: The memo names need as its only criterion and mentions identity in order to deny that it counts. Its own lists of activities and inputs include data collection on access and real-time tracking in nominal form, with the collectors and the tracked persons left unnamed.

ex.t: Aid will be distributed without regard to identity, origin, or affiliation. There will be no eligibility requirements—assistance will be delivered purely based on need, with community dignity and safety as top priorities.
ex.v: Memo, section on operations. The preceding sentence states that the IDF will not be stationed at the sites.

a.n: The agentless passive with ‘will’ leaves the distributor implicit in a sentence about the foundation’s own operation.
The memo names identity in order to deny that it counts, while its list of activities includes data collection on access.
A categorical negative prediction rules out any condition of access.
Need appears as the sole criterion, a legitimation drawn from humanitarian principle.

ex.t: Collect data on aid delivery, access, and recipient feedback
ex.v: Memo, list of ‘Activities’.

a.n: The bare verb in a list omits both the collector and the persons whose data is collected.
Access is an object of data collection, which leaves open whether the data concern numbers or persons.
People are named by their relation to aid, as ‘recipients’ whose feedback becomes data.

ex.t: Technology for real-time tracking and reporting
ex.v: Memo, list of inputs.

a.n: The nominalised ‘tracking’ leaves open what or whom the technology tracks.

ex.t: We serve people based solely on necessity, without discrimination or bias.
ex.v: Memo, statement of values.

a.n: The organisational ‘we’ activates the foundation as a moral agent.
Necessity here names the recipients’ need and serves as the sole stated criterion.
Neutrality is asserted through the denial of two negative qualities.

ex.t: the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) will not be stationed at or near SDS locations
ex.v: Memo, after the statement that perimeter security will be provided by ‘experienced professionals’.

a.n: The army is the passivated object of stationing, and the authority that stations it is unnamed.
A categorical future negative states the army’s absence as certain.
The initialism abbreviates the memo’s ‘safe, neutral aid distribution sites’, so the evaluation is built into the name of the sites.

docs.title: Permanent Representative of Israel, letter to the President of the Security Council (S/2025/313), with Fletcher’s letter annexed
docs.voice: Security Council document with two letters. Annex I is Ambassador Danny Danon to Tom Fletcher, and annex II is Fletcher to Danon, dated 16 May 2025.
docs.profile: Danon’s letter presents aid as a resumption granted by cabinet approval and justified by looting that it presupposes. Fletcher’s reply speaks of verification measures against theft by Hamas, so both letters share the premise that aid and its recipients must be checked.

ex.t: the Israeli Security Cabinet has approved the resumption of aid entry into Gaza facilitated by specific agencies with strict oversight to prevent Hamas’ continued looting of humanitarian resources.
ex.v: Danny Danon, annex I, after ‘That is why, after careful deliberation,’.

a.n: Aid depends on the approval of an activated state authority, which legitimates the arrangement by its institutional standing.
Stacked nominalisations present the end of a stoppage without naming who stopped aid from entering.
The agencies are marked as specific and yet remain unnamed in the letter.
Control appears as a nominalised and intensified quality of the arrangement.
The purpose relation legitimates oversight by the harm it prevents.
The nominal group presupposes that looting by Hamas exists and continues, so the claim enters the letter as given.

ex.t: We have solid plans to distribute to civilians, with verification measures to ensure that aid does not get stolen by Hamas.
ex.v: Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, annex II.

a.n: The UN’s ‘we’ claims the capacity to deliver.
The attribute asserts the reliability of the UN’s plans.
The UN coordinator also uses the vocabulary of verification, so the premise of checking appears on both sides of the exchange.
The purpose clause accepts the possibility of theft by Hamas that the Israeli letter presupposes.

docs.title: US Embassy Jerusalem, ‘Ambassador Huckabee’s Interview with CBS News’
docs.voice: Interview transcript published by the US Embassy, with the CBS reporter’s questions and Ambassador Huckabee’s answers.
docs.profile: The exchange turns on the reporter’s presupposition that recipients might be members of Hamas. The ambassador concedes that no guarantee is possible, then asserts an agentless screening and narrows its purpose to weapons, which leaves the question of identity unanswered.

ex.t: How do we know that those people aren’t from Hamas?
ex.v: CBS reporter, question to the ambassador.

a.n: The reporter’s ‘we’ places questioner and audience among those entitled to know who receives aid.
Recipients appear as ‘those people’, held at a distance by the demonstrative.
The question presupposes that recipients may belong to Hamas and that their affiliation should be known.

ex.t: You can’t absolutely guarantee that they’re not
ex.v: Ambassador Huckabee, answer.

a.n: Generic ‘you’ extends the impossibility to anyone who might attempt a guarantee.
The negated modal with an intensifier concedes that recipients cannot be cleared.
The elliptical clause takes over the reporter’s presupposition without restating it.

ex.t: But there’s zero verification process.
ex.v: CBS reporter, follow-up.

a.n: The numeral ‘zero’ states the absence with full commitment.
The reporter makes verification the measure of adequate aid, the frame within which the ambassador then answers.

ex.t: Look, no, there is a screening that is done.
ex.v: Ambassador Huckabee, answer.

a.n: The discourse markers signal disagreement before the claim and raise its assertive force.
Screening is named as a noun, without its agent or its object.
The agentless passive repeats the absence of a screener.

ex.t: There’s a screening to make sure they’re not carrying weapons.
ex.v: Ambassador Huckabee, after the reporter asks ‘What is that screening?’.

a.n: The purpose clause redefines the screening as a check for weapons, so the answer moves from identity to objects.
Recipients remain an undifferentiated ‘they’.

docs.title: UN Geneva press briefing, teleprompter transcript (UNICEF)
docs.voice: James Elder for UNICEF, speaking at the briefing. The transcript has no speaker labels, so the speaker is identified from the briefing summary and the surrounding remarks in the same file.
docs.profile: UNICEF’s objection is carried by an institutional ‘we’ and by affective and moral evaluation. Recipients appear as passivated ‘beneficiaries’, and the evaluation ‘impossible choice’ names the absence of the genuine choice that the node’s definition of consent requires.

ex.t: It appears designed to reinforce control over life sustaining items as a pressure tactic.
ex.v: James Elder (UNICEF), on the distribution plan.

a.n: The evidential ‘appears’ lowers commitment to a claim about the plan’s design.
The participle implies a designer who remains unnamed.
The purpose attributed to the plan is control over goods needed for life.
The phrase evaluates the plan as coercive.

ex.t: Finally, we are very concerned about the proposal to use facial recognition as a as a precondition to access aid.
ex.v: James Elder (UNICEF). The repetition ‘as a as a’ is in the transcript.

a.n: The objecting subject is UNICEF’s ‘we’, so the contestation belongs to an institution.
An affective mental process, intensified by ‘very’, carries the objection (Fairclough 2003, p. 173).
The nominalisation leaves the author of the plan unnamed.
The noun names the conditionality to which the speaker objects.

ex.t: It's against all humanitarian principles to screen and monitor beneficiaries for intelligence and military purposes.
ex.v: James Elder (UNICEF), the next sentence.

a.n: The objection appeals to principle, and the universal ‘all’ raises its commitment.
Beneficiaries are the passivated objects of screening and monitoring, with the screener unnamed.
The purpose phrase names the uses that the speaker attributes to the screening.

ex.t: will create this impossible choice between displacement and death.
ex.v: James Elder (UNICEF). The subject is ‘the use of humanitarian aid as a bait to force displacement’.

a.n: A categorical prediction presents the outcome as certain.
The evaluation names a choice in name only, the opposite of the ‘genuine choice’ in the node’s definition of consent.
Two nominalisations name the alternatives without naming who displaces or who dies.

docs.pos: Voice of those subject to it
docs.title: Reuters, ‘Palestinians rush US-backed aid centre despite concerns over checks’
docs.voice: Reuters report, saved from Stabroek News, with direct speech from Abu Ahmed, 55, a father of seven, and reported speech from humanitarian groups.
docs.profile: The report attributes the checks to Israel through indirect speech and gives agency to nominalised states of desperation and concern. In direct speech the father’s hunger and fear share one concessive sentence, and the reported condition requires ‘anyone’ to ‘submit’.

ex.t: with desperation for food overcoming concern about biometric and other checks Israel said it would employ.
ex.v: Lead sentence. The main clause reports that thousands of Palestinians rushed a distribution site.

a.n: Two nominalised states act as participants, so the clause attributes the decision to go to desperation and concern.
The vague ‘other checks’ widens the category beyond biometrics.
The checks are attributed to Israel through reported speech, which reports the statement without quoting it.

ex.t: As much as I want to go because I am hungry and my children are hungry, I am afraid,
ex.v: Abu Ahmed, 55, a father of seven, direct speech.

a.n: The concessive frame sets desire against fear inside one sentence.
The reason clause grounds the wish to go in hunger, his own and his children’s.
Fear is the speaker’s stated state, and the sentence contains no clause of refusal.

ex.t: anyone accessing aid will have to submit to facial recognition technology
ex.v: Reported speech attributed to ‘Humanitarian groups briefed on the foundation’s plans’.

a.n: The generic ‘anyone’ extends the condition to every recipient.
The deontic ‘have to’ marks the condition as compulsory.
The verb ‘submit’ positions the recipient as subordinate to the technology.

docs.title: Ministry of Home Affairs, media statement on the Minister’s visit to the Bidor centre
docs.voice: Ministry press statement in Malay, written in the third person about the working visit of the Minister of Home Affairs, Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution bin Ismail.
docs.profile: The ministry names the government by its MADANI brand and evaluates refugee management as ‘terkawal’ (controlled) and ‘berperikemanusiaan’ (humane) in one series. Legitimation runs through a National Security Council directive and ‘valid data’, while people appear as migrants and as detainees who have been entered as data.

ex.t: Pusat Pengasingan Khas Pelarian dan Pemohon Suaka (PPKPPS) Bidor
ex.v: Name of the centre in the statement’s first paragraph.

a.n: ‘Pengasingan’ means separation or isolation, so the place where the programme runs is named as a place that separates refugees.

ex.gl: Special Separation Centre for Refugees and Asylum Seekers (PPKPPS), Bidor

ex.t: Program DPP merupakan pendekatan baharu Kerajaan MADANI dalam mengurus pelarian dan pemohon suaka secara lebih tersusun, terkawal dan berperikemanusiaan
ex.v: Statement, paragraph 1.

a.n: The government names itself by its political brand, so the programme is attributed to a branded administration.
‘Mengurus’ (managing) makes refugees and asylum seekers the objects of administration.
The series joins ‘terkawal’ (controlled) to ‘berperikemanusiaan’ (humane), so control and care are evaluated together as qualities of one approach.

ex.gl: The DPP Programme is a new approach of the MADANI Government to managing refugees and asylum seekers in a more orderly, controlled and humane manner

ex.t: selaras dengan Arahan Majlis Keselamatan Negara No. 23 (Semakan 2023), tanpa menjejaskan aspek keselamatan serta kedaulatan negara.
ex.v: Statement, end of paragraph 1.

a.n: The programme is legitimated by a security directive, which places refugee management within national security.
The clause ‘without compromising’ presupposes that refugee management could threaten security and sovereignty.

ex.gl: in line with National Security Council Directive No. 23 (Revision 2023), without compromising the security and sovereignty of the nation.

ex.t: membolehkan Kerajaan merekod maklumat identiti dan biometrik migran yang memerlukan perlindungan sementara, sekali gus memperkukuh keupayaan pemantauan, penguatkuasaan dan perancangan dasar berasaskan data yang sahih.
ex.v: Statement, paragraph 2, after ‘Pelaksanaan program ini’ (the implementation of this programme).

a.n: The government is the activated recorder, so this text names the agency that holds the data.
People are ‘migrants’ who need ‘temporary protection’, although the programme’s own name speaks of refugees (‘pelarian’).
The connective ‘sekali gus’ (thereby) presents monitoring and enforcement as results of recording.
Nominalised monitoring and enforcement name state capacities without stating whom they are directed at.
‘Valid data’ legitimates the programme by its utility for policy.

ex.gl: enables the Government to record the identity and biometric information of migrants who need temporary protection, thereby strengthening the capacity for monitoring, enforcement and policy planning based on valid data.

ex.t: Setakat ini, seramai 4,010 tahanan telah didatakan
ex.v: Statement, paragraph 3.

a.n: People are counted as ‘tahanan’ (detainees), so detention defines them at the moment of registration.
The passive verb is formed on the noun ‘data’ and names no agent, so detainees become the objects of a process named after data.

ex.gl: So far, a total of 4,010 detainees have been entered as data

docs.title: UNHCR Malaysia, ‘Important update on Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (DPP) Programme’
docs.voice: UNHCR Malaysia web notice in English, addressed to refugees.
docs.profile: The agency presents itself as a recipient of information and relays the government’s plan without naming its source. It evaluates legitimacy by place, so registration inside detention becomes the legitimate form, and it refers readers to the ministry for official information.

ex.t: UNHCR has been informed that the first phase of the Government’s Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (DPP) programme will focus on registering individuals currently held in immigration detention centres.
ex.v: Notice, opening sentence under ‘Registration’.

a.n: The agentless ‘has been informed’ relays the plan without naming the informant and casts UNHCR as a recipient of information.
The possessive assigns the programme to the government.
Individuals are the objects of registering and of being held, and the holding authority is unnamed.

ex.t: Please note that anyone claiming to represent the Government to register refugees under the DPP programme OUTSIDE of detention facilities is not legitimate.
ex.v: Notice, second sentence.

a.n: The imperative addresses refugees directly with a demand for attention.
Capitals stress location, so detention becomes the place of legitimate registration.
The agency evaluates legitimacy by location, which implies that registration inside detention is the legitimate form.

ex.t: For official updates and further information on the DPP programme, please refer to the Ministry of Home Affairs social media channels
ex.v: Notice, third sentence, followed by links to the ministry’s Facebook pages.

a.n: The attribute ‘official’ assigns authority to the ministry’s updates.
The notice sends readers to the ministry’s channels, so the government becomes the authoritative source on the programme.

docs.title: Dewan Negara Hansard, sitting of 23 July 2026
docs.voice: Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dato Lukanisman bin Awang Sauni, answering question 6 from Senator Rita Sarimah anak Patrick Insol and the supplementary questions that followed.
docs.profile: The deputy minister speaks as a government ‘kita’ (we) that instructs UNHCR and lists expulsion among ‘long-term solutions’. His answer presupposes card misuse by Rohingya refugees and limits humane acceptance to the present. It also denies that finding resettlement places is the government’s responsibility.

ex.t: kita juga telah pun mengarahkan agar pihak UNHCR untuk menghentikan sebarang pendaftaran pelarian ketika ini, di mana kita sedang dalam proses untuk menyusun semula program DPP yang kita perkenalkan.
ex.v: Deputy minister, after ‘melalui keputusan Kabinet’ (through a Cabinet decision).

a.n: The government’s ‘kita’ (we) is the activated agent that instructs.
‘Mengarahkan’ (instructed) makes UNHCR the recipient of a government directive, which reverses the node’s position of the agency as the setter of standards.
Registration is nominalised and quantified by ‘sebarang’ (any), so the instruction covers all registration.
The relative clause claims the programme as the government’s own (‘that we introduced’).

ex.gl: we have also instructed UNHCR to stop any registration of refugees at this time, as we are in the process of restructuring the DPP programme that we introduced.

ex.t: pemindahan ataupun pengusiran tindakan mandatori akibat pelanggaran undang-undang tempatan.
ex.v: Deputy minister, the third of ‘tiga penyelesaian jangka panjang’ (three long-term solutions), after repatriation and resettlement.

a.n: Expulsion is listed as a ‘long-term solution’, the place that local integration holds among UNHCR’s durable solutions.
The borrowed ‘mandatori’ marks expulsion as obligatory action.
‘Akibat’ (as a result of) attaches expulsion to the person’s act.
The violation is nominalised, and ‘local law’ echoes the Bangladesh FAQ on ‘adherence to local laws’.

ex.gl: transfer or expulsion as mandatory action resulting from violations of local law.

ex.t: Di mana kita tidak ingin melihat bahawa pelarian-pelarian khususnya Rohingya ini menyalahgunakan kad UNHCR yang sedia ada.
ex.v: Deputy minister, after ‘kad DPP itu adalah sangat-sangat penting’ (the DPP card is very, very important).

a.n: A negated desiderative (‘do not wish to see’) states the government’s stance as a wish.
The reduplicated plural and the demonstrative ‘ini’ (these) single out the Rohingya as a group.
The clause presupposes misuse of UNHCR cards by refugees, which justifies the government’s own card.

ex.gl: Since we do not wish to see these refugees, particularly the Rohingya, misusing the existing UNHCR cards.

ex.t: Demi kemanusiaan kita menerima pelarian Rohingya ketika ini, tetapi kita kena memikirkan kesejahteraan rakyat kita
ex.v: Deputy minister, closing an answer to a supplementary question.

a.n: Acceptance is legitimated by humanity, and ‘ketika ini’ (at this time) limits it to the present.
The contrastive ‘tetapi’ (but) sets humanity against the welfare of citizens.
‘Kena’ (must) expresses an obligation that runs to citizens.
‘Rakyat kita’ (our people) separates citizens from refugees through the possessive.

ex.gl: For the sake of humanity we accept Rohingya refugees at this time, but we must think of the welfare of our people

ex.t: Bukan tanggungjawab Kerajaan Malaysia untuk mencari negara ketiga untuk penempatan Rohingya ini.
ex.v: Deputy minister, after saying that resettlement is ‘tanggungjawab UNHCR’ (UNHCR’s responsibility).

a.n: The negated noun of responsibility assigns the task of resettlement to UNHCR, named in the previous sentence.
Resettlement is nominalised with the Rohingya as its object.

ex.gl: It is not the responsibility of the Government of Malaysia to find a third country for the resettlement of these Rohingya.

docs.title: UNHCR, ‘UNHCR concerned by returns from Malaysia to Myanmar amid ongoing conflict’
docs.voice: UNHCR press release with direct quotations from Edem Wosornu, Assistant High Commissioner for Protection.
docs.profile: UNHCR attributes voluntariness to the authorities in reported speech and questions it with low commitment, grounding its doubt in a lack of access. It then restates the standard as a high deontic ‘must’ with no named addressee and places valid assessment outside detention.

ex.t: While authorities say the returns are voluntary, those returned had been held in immigration detention.
ex.v: Edem Wosornu, direct quotation.

a.n: The contrastive ‘while’ sets the authorities’ claim against the fact of detention.
The claim of voluntariness is attributed to unnamed ‘authorities’, which marks it as theirs and lowers the speaker’s commitment to it (Fairclough 2003, p. 171).
Returnees appear only as objects of return and detention, and the detaining authority is unnamed.

ex.t: This raises serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed.
ex.v: Edem Wosornu, direct quotation.

a.n: The speaker questions voluntariness without asserting coercion, a lower commitment than a categorical claim.
Return is nominalised as ‘decisions’, which keeps the frame of individual choice.
The phrase restates the guidance’s ‘Freely given’ and ‘genuine choice’ and applies them to return.

ex.t: UNHCR did not have access to the individuals to assess this.
ex.v: Edem Wosornu, direct quotation.

a.n: The agency is the subject of a negated process, so the text states the limit of its own knowledge.
The negative statement explains the low commitment of the previous sentence.

ex.t: Decisions to return must be voluntary and assessed outside detention settings.
ex.v: Press release narrative, after ‘UNHCR urges Malaysia to ensure’.

a.n: High deontic ‘must’ restates voluntariness as an obligation addressed to no named agent.
The agentless ‘assessed’ leaves open who assesses.
The phrase places valid assessment outside detention, while UNHCR Malaysia’s notice placed legitimate registration inside it.

docs.pos: Voice of those subject to it
docs.title: Myanmar Now, ‘Myanmar nationals in Malaysia fear arrest and forced return’
docs.voice: News report with direct speech from James Bawi Thang Bik, chair of the Kuala Lumpur-based Alliance of Chin Refugees.
docs.profile: The report places ‘voluntarily’ in scare quotes at the end of a chain of agentless passives. The community leader marks the authorities’ statement as a claim and names detention centres as prisons. He rejects the inference from a signature to voluntariness.

ex.t: being arrested, detained, and “voluntarily” returned
ex.v: Journalist’s narrative. The subject is Myanmar nationals ‘lacking legal documentation’.

a.n: Agentless passives present arrest and detention as things done to people, with no authority named.
Scare quotes mark ‘voluntarily’ as the authorities’ word and distance the report from it.

ex.t: They always claim they are sending them back voluntarily, but we don’t know what pressure they face inside the prisons.
ex.v: James Bawi Thang Bik, direct speech.

a.n: The verb ‘claim’ marks the authorities’ statement as contestable, and ‘always’ marks it as repeated.
The contrast sets the claim against what cannot be known.
The speaker states a limit of knowledge, the same ground UNHCR gives for its doubt.
Detention centres are named ‘prisons’.

ex.t: Just because there is a signature on a piece of paper doesn’t make it voluntary,
ex.v: James Bawi Thang Bik, direct speech.

a.n: The speaker rejects the causal inference from signature to voluntariness.
The phrase diminishes the document that the authorities treat as proof of consent.

docs.title: Minister of Social Development, SRD Regulations (GN R2042 of 2022), regulation 4(2)
docs.voice: Regulation made by the Minister of Social Development. Legal text.
docs.profile: The regulation turns the act of applying into consent, so the applicant is the grammatical subject of consenting while the text supplies the consent. Necessity appears twice without a named judge, and disclosure extends to an open class of institutions.

ex.t: By virtue of application for the Covid-19 Social Relief of Distress, an applicant consents to the Agency or the Independent Tribunal, when necessary, to process, including collecting, verifying, using and disclosing the information of the applicant
ex.v: Regulation 4(2), headed ‘Date of application and consent by applicant to information sharing’.

a.n: The nominalised act of applying is the ground from which consent follows, so applying counts as consenting.
The applicant is the grammatical subject of consenting, although the regulation produces the consent.
Necessity is stated without saying who judges it.
A series of gerunds names the data processes, with the Agency as their implied agent.

ex.t: any other government or private institution considered necessary.
ex.v: Regulation 4(2)(d), the last item in the list of bodies.

a.n: The open category extends disclosure beyond the bodies named in the list.
The agentless ‘considered’ leaves the judge of necessity unnamed.

docs.title: SAnews, ‘SASSA to introduce biometric enrolment in September’
docs.voice: Government news agency report of a SASSA statement.
docs.profile: The government news service reports compulsion as an announcement and legitimates enrolment by its purpose of making recipients verifiably authentic. Applicants appear as applications and clients, and missing data leads automatically to review through agentless passives.

ex.t: The South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) has announced that it will be introducing mandatory Beneficiary Biometric Enrolment at all its offices from 01 September 2025.
ex.v: Opening sentence.

a.n: The government news service reports SASSA’s announcement in indirect speech and takes no distance from it.
The deontic adjective attaches compulsion to enrolment.
Capitalisation turns the process into a named programme in which beneficiaries become a modifier.

ex.t: detect and effectively root out any fraudulent elements in social grant administration.
ex.v: Third paragraph. The subject is the agency ‘ramping up efforts to improve its systems’.

a.n: The verb ‘root out’ presents fraud as embedded and in need of removal.
The phrase assumes that fraudulent elements exist, without saying who they are.

ex.t: biometric enrolment is a strategic move to ensure every grant recipient is verifiably authentic
ex.v: Third paragraph, after ‘Moreover,’.

a.n: Enrolment is evaluated as strategy.
The purpose relation legitimates enrolment by its utility.
Every recipient becomes the object of verification.
The phrase assumes that a recipient’s authenticity is open to doubt until verified.

ex.t: Applications without biometric data will be immediately put into the review cycle, notifying the client of the need to capture biometrics as per the review processes.
ex.v: Later paragraph, after the list of expected benefits.

a.n: Applicants appear as ‘applications’, an impersonal representation (Fairclough 2003, p. 146).
The prepositional phrase works as a condition, so missing data triggers review.
The agentless passive with ‘immediately’ presents the consequence as automatic.
Grant recipients are named ‘clients’, a term from commercial service.
The nominalised ‘need’ states the obligation without its source.

docs.title: Open Secrets, ‘Digital Profiteers (Part Two)’, with a SASSA official on consent
docs.voice: Civil society investigation quoting Brenton van Vrede, SASSA Executive Grants Manager, from a 2025 interview, in answer to a question on informed consent.
docs.profile: The official places responsibility for informed consent on whether the person reads the terms. Conditionals and negated possibility make consent the only route to assessment, and the agency’s refusal to assess appears as an incapacity (‘we can’t’).

ex.t: It really depends on whether the person reads it
ex.v: Brenton van Vrede, answering whether the forms provide informed consent.

a.n: Informed consent is made conditional on the applicant’s reading.
The person is the activated reader, so responsibility for being informed falls on the applicant.

ex.t: There’s no way you can proceed with the application if you don’t accept the T&C’s
ex.v: Brenton van Vrede, after comparing applicants with ‘most of us’ when ‘we want something’.

a.n: Negated possibility closes every route except acceptance.
The conditional makes acceptance the condition of proceeding.
The consumer form of terms and conditions frames an application for a social grant.

ex.t: which might not sound fair, but… if you don’t consent, we can’t assess you.
ex.v: Brenton van Vrede, end of the answer.

a.n: Low epistemic ‘might’ with ‘sound’ concedes unfairness as an appearance only.
The contrast sets fairness aside in favour of the condition.
The conditional makes consent the condition of assessment.
The negated ‘can’ presents the agency’s refusal to assess as an incapacity, with ‘we’ as the agency.

docs.title: High Court, Institute for Economic Justice v Minister of Social Development [2025] ZAGPPHC 29
docs.voice: Judgment of the High Court, Gauteng Division, Pretoria, delivered by Twala J.
docs.profile: The court adopts the state’s term ‘safeguards’ and evaluates it against reasonableness and fairness with high deontic commitment. It classifies beneficiaries as poor and vulnerable and attributes an exclusionary purpose to verification, so the purpose relation that legitimates the condition in SASSA’s texts becomes the ground of the court’s finding against it.

ex.t: It cannot be right to promulgate regulations with safeguards that are intended to reduce the number of people who are eligible for the SRD grant
ex.v: Paragraph 94.

a.n: A negated evaluation with high commitment judges the regulations as wrong.
The court reads the safeguards by their purpose, which it names as reducing eligibility.

ex.t: The safeguards must be reasonable and fair.
ex.v: Paragraph 94, closing sentence.

a.n: The court takes over the state’s word ‘safeguards’ and makes it the object of evaluation.
High deontic ‘must’ binds the safeguards to legal standards.
The attributes come from administrative law and set the measure for the rest of the judgment.

ex.t: There is no reasonable justification to subject its potential beneficiaries, who are mainly poor and vulnerable members of society, to a solely online application process.
ex.v: Paragraph 95.

a.n: The court denies the legitimation that the state offers for the online process.
Beneficiaries are the objects of ‘subject’, a verb that marks the process as imposed.
The relative clause classifies beneficiaries by poverty and vulnerability, which ties the evaluation to the people affected.

ex.t: The databases verification process is therefore unreasonable and unfair and is used with an ulterior purpose of excluding eligible SRD grant applicants from receiving it.
ex.v: Paragraph 125.

a.n: The conclusion follows from the preceding reasoning on database checks.
The negative attributes answer the standard ‘reasonable and fair’ of paragraph 94.
The agentless ‘is used’ backgrounds the agency, which the context identifies as SASSA.
The court attributes an exclusionary purpose to verification, the relation that SASSA’s texts use to legitimate it.

docs.pos: Voice of those subject to it
docs.title: GroundUp, ‘SASSA’s new ID verification process sparks alarm’
docs.voice: News report with direct speech from Lerverch Pieters, an SRD grant recipient, and from Paseka Letsatsi, SASSA spokesperson.
docs.profile: The agency’s justification appears in reported speech as a purpose of fighting fraud. The recipient’s question challenges the necessity of a repeated check, and the spokesperson answers with a categorical prediction that grants will remain suspended.

ex.t: SASSA spokesperson Paseka Letsatsi says the process has been introduced to fight fraud.
ex.v: Article summary at the head of the report.

a.n: The agency’s justification is reported indirectly in the article’s summary.
The agentless passive leaves the introducing authority implicit.
Fraud prevention legitimates the process by its purpose.

ex.t: The relevant cross-checks have been done with your bank account to verify if it’s you, why do they need to verify your identity again?
ex.v: Lerverch Pieters, direct speech. The journalist notes that his grant is paid into his bank account.

a.n: The recipient also uses an agentless passive for the checks.
‘They’ names the agency as an unspecified other.
The question challenges the necessity that the agency claims.
‘Again’ frames the verification as redundant.

ex.t: Their grants will remain suspended
ex.v: Paseka Letsatsi, asked what will happen to recipients who do not complete the verification.

a.n: Recipients appear only as the possessors of grants.
A categorical prediction with an agentless participle states the consequence as a continuing state.

docs.title: ThePrint, ‘“Our blood”: Mizoram won’t collect biometric data of Myanmar refugees as ordered by Centre’ (the state government’s refusal, as reported)
docs.voice: News report by Isaac Zoramsanga on the state government’s decision, with Minister Lalruatkima’s statement to the media.
docs.profile: The report activates the state, named as ‘Mizoram’, as the agent of refusal and grounds the refusal in a predicted harm. The central instruction appears in the minister’s reported speech, which makes the hierarchy between centre and state explicit.

ex.t: Mizoram has decided not to collect biometric and biographic data of Myanmar refugees in the state as it would lead to discrimination.
ex.v: Opening sentence, datelined Aizawl.

a.n: The state, named as ‘Mizoram’, is the activated agent of refusal.
The hypothetical ‘would’ frames discrimination as the expected result of collection.
The reason clause grounds the refusal in a predicted harm.

ex.t: the Union Ministry of Home Affairs had instructed the Mizoram government to collect biographic and biometric data of Myanmar refugees.
ex.v: Reported speech after ‘Lalruatkima told the media that’.

a.n: The Union ministry is the activated agent of the instruction, so the hierarchy between centre and state is explicit.
The past perfect marks indirect speech, so the directive reaches the reader through the minister’s report.

docs.pos: Voice of those subject to it
docs.title: The Wire (Myanmar Now report), ‘Fear, Mistrust Grow as India Collects Biometrics From Myanmar Refugees’
docs.voice: Report with direct speech from Siamliana, a pseudonym in the report, a 57-year-old resident, and a quotation from the former chief minister Zoramthanga.
docs.profile: The report carries the central ‘mandate’ through local leaders to residents. In direct speech the resident’s refusal appears only as the object of fear, while the former chief minister’s kinship vocabulary places refugees inside the political community.

ex.t: village council leaders arrived with an Indian government mandate to enrol residents in a biometric identification process.
ex.v: Journalist’s narrative.

a.n: Local leaders are the activated carriers of the central instruction.
The deontic noun comes from the national government and arrives through local leaders.
People are named ‘residents’, a term that places them in the village.

ex.t: We do not know what use it will have for us, but we are afraid to refuse the mandate,
ex.v: Siamliana (pseudonym), direct speech.

a.n: The speaker states a lack of knowledge about the purpose of the enrolment.
The contrast sets that uncertainty against fear.
Refusal appears as the object of fear, so the person’s refusal remains a possibility only.

ex.t: discrimination against people who are of our blood and kindred brothers and sisters.
ex.v: Former chief minister Zoramthanga, quoted by the report.

a.n: The nominalisation evaluates the collection as harmful without naming who would discriminate.
Kinship vocabulary includes the refugees in the speaker’s own group.

missing.title: Ministry of Home Affairs (Delhi), directive on biometrics of Myanmar nationals
Government of Mizoram, statement on the enrolment
Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha answer on the enrolment

readings.title: Implementing texts leave out who decides loss
p: In the texts that set or run the condition, the processes that decide loss appear as agentless passives or nominalisations. Examples are ‘will be inactivated’, ‘deregistration’, ‘will be immediately put into the review cycle’ and ‘didatakan’. The Diplomat repeats the pattern when it reports that families ‘have been cut off’ from food aid.

People appear as generic or negatively defined classes, in the implementing texts and in reports of them, for example ‘all eligible persons’, ‘every grant recipient’, ‘anyone accessing aid’ and ‘those not biometrically registered’.

Agents appear when a text contests the condition or when a government speaks in its own name. ThePrint makes ‘the Union Ministry of Home Affairs’ the instructing agent, and in the Senate the government’s ‘kita’ (we) instructs UNHCR in the first person.

readings.title: From ‘voluntary’ to ‘required’
p: The node states that ‘participation in registration is voluntary’ and permits registration without biometrics with ‘may’. The Bangladesh notice keeps the nominalisation and changes its attribute to ‘required’. The same move appears as ‘mandatory’ in the SASSA announcement and as ‘tindakan mandatori’ in the Senate, and the Reuters report gives it as ‘will have to’.

The node itself contains both terms of this shift. Its list places ‘their obligation to cooperate’ next to voluntariness, and in a footnote the guidance assigns ‘the requirement to share personal data’ to government policy wherever a government leads registration.

readings.title: Loss attached to the person’s act
p: The node detaches refusal from loss with ‘without adverse consequences’. The implementing texts attach loss to the person’s act through relations of consequence and condition. The examples run from ‘Persons who fail to show up will be inactivated’ in Bangladesh to ‘if you don’t consent, we can’t assess you’ in South Africa.

In these clauses the person’s act is the first link of the chain, while the deciding agency is absent or appears as an incapacity. This is the textual form of the responsibility that RQ1 asks about, because the person who must choose becomes the grammatical cause of the outcome.

readings.title: Institutions refuse, people fear
p: Refusal is the person’s own act in two texts only, the node’s ‘right to refuse’ and the report in The Diplomat of families ‘refusing to participate’. In the contesting texts the refuser is an institution, as in ‘Mizoram has decided not to collect’, UNICEF’s ‘we are very concerned’, UNHCR’s ‘raises serious questions’ and the court’s ‘unreasonable and unfair’.

In the voices of those subject to the condition, refusal appears as fear, in ‘we are afraid to refuse the mandate’. It also appears as a question about necessity, in ‘why do they need to verify your identity again?’. For RQ2, recognition would have to answer refusal by persons, and these texts rarely make such refusal the act of a grammatical subject.

readings.title: Consent words against verification words
p: The vocabulary of consent recurs in the contesting texts. UNHCR’s ‘genuinely free and informed’ restates the guidance, and the Chin community leader denies that a signature makes return ‘voluntary’.

The implementing texts speak of verification and fraud, in ‘verification measures’, ‘verifiably authentic’, ‘fraudulent elements’ and ‘menyalahgunakan kad UNHCR’ (misusing UNHCR cards). Where consent appears on the implementing side, the SRD regulation deems it from the act of applying, and the Terms tab gives the distribution of both vocabularies across the 21 documents.

readings.title: Tensions inside the UN system
p: UN texts both contest the condition and adopt its premise. In Gaza, UNICEF objects on 9 May 2025 to plans ‘to screen and monitor beneficiaries’. On 16 May the Emergency Relief Coordinator promises ‘verification measures to ensure that aid does not get stolen by Hamas’.

In Malaysia, UNHCR’s January notice treats registration ‘OUTSIDE of detention facilities’ as illegitimate, while UNHCR’s September release requires that decisions to return be ‘assessed outside detention settings’. In Bangladesh, the guidance’s ‘without adverse consequences’ stands beside the joint FAQ’s ‘discontinuation of protection and assistance’.

readings.title: Who counts as ‘our people’
p: Speakers in the Malaysian Senate and in Mizoram use collective pronouns to exclude or to include refugees. In the Senate, ‘rakyat kita’ (our people) separates citizens from refugees whose acceptance holds only ‘ketika ini’ (at this time).

In Mizoram, the former chief minister calls the refugees people ‘of our blood and kindred brothers and sisters’ and names collection as discrimination against them. In the Huckabee interview, the reporter’s ‘we’ and ‘those people’ place recipients outside the community that is entitled to know.
